Highly Chemoselective Esterification from O-Aminoallylation of
Carboxylic Acids:M etal- and Reagent-Free Hydrocarboxylation of
Allenamides
TapasR .P radhan+,[a] Hae Eun Lee+,[a] Gisela A. Gonzalez-Montiel,[b] Paul Ha-Yeon Cheong,*[b]
and Jin Kyoon Park*[a]
Abstract: Metal-free hydrocarboxylation of allenamides with
various functionalized carboxylic acids were achieved with
complete regio- and stereocontrol (> 49:1). This environ-
mentally compatible transformation affords g-acyloxyen-
amides with exclusive E-selectivity.E lectron rich, electron
poor,a liphatic, aryl, and heterocyclic carboxylic acids all
gave excellent yields (avg. 89 %, 47 examples). We demon-
strate the synthetic potentialo ft his transformation in the
late-stage modification of complex natural carboxylic acids
and simple modification of the products to three-carbon
synthons with ample opportunity for further diversification.
DFT studies revealed that the reaction occurs in as tepwise
mannert hrough the intermediacy of ac onjugated iminum
species, which is rapidly captured by the carboxylate ion, re-
sulting in the observed linear selectivity.
Introduction
The importance of ester groups has been highlighted by many
applicationsi nd rug discovery,[1] polymerization,[2] and electron-
ic material development.[3] Enamide groups have received par-
ticular attention as versatile ambiphilic building blocks[4] for
biologically relevant molecules, including therapeutically im-
portant natural products and drug molecules.[5] Herein, we dis-
close am ethodf or the direct O-aminoallylation of carboxylic
acid groups using allenamides to afford highly functionalizable
enamide derivatives.[6] This atom-economical method exhibits
ab road substrate scope, exclusive chemo-, regio-, and E-selec-
tivities. Our processt ransforms several inexpensive, stable, and
abundant carboxylic acids into synthetically valuable g-acyloxy-
enamides.T he mild reactionc onditions, exclusivec hemoselec-
tivity,a nd wide functional group tolerance also provide ready
access to late-stage functionalization of complex natural prod-
ucts bearing carboxylic acids. This chemoselective functionali-
zation is ap owerful way to construct libraries of novel chemi-
cal entities from simple and complex carboxylic acid sub-
strates,[7] enabling rapid exploration for structure–activity rela-
tionship (SAR).
The uniquec hemical features of allenes have inspired nu-
merous atom- and step-economic strategies for constructing
organic compounds including valuable synthons and polyfunc-
tional structures.[8] Despite the great success of transition-
metal catalysis, sustainable metal-free processes are increasing-
ly in demand because of clear disadvantages of metals, such
as:t oxicityo fm etals, cost and poor availability of ligands, and
hazardousness of additives. Meanwhile, Brønsted acid electro-
philic activation of allenesa sa greener alternative to transition
metal functionalization are relativelyr are.[9] In particular, hydro-
carboxylation, which enables the synthesis of linear or
brancheda llyl ester derivatives, under metal-free conditions re-
mains unknown (Scheme 1( A)). We report herein ag reener al-
ternative to the currents tate-of-the-art process, am etal-free
hydrocarboxylation (Scheme 1( B)), which could be used for ef-
ficientl ate-stage functionalization.
Transition-metal catalysts typically activate neutral
(Scheme 1( A), top). For example, iridium and rhodium[9b,c] cata-
lyst processes that produce branched products have been re-
portedi ndependently by Krische[9a] and Breit.[9b,c] On the other
hand, regiocontrolled synthesis of linear products with trans
selectivity from allenesh as been realizedb yG uo[9d] and Yama-
moto,[9e,f] using silver and palladium catalysts, respectively.
Most interestingly,l iteratures on transformationsi nvolving the
allenamides are scarce. The one exception is the recent report
of ac opper-catalyzed hydrocarboxylation of allenamides dis-
covered by the Monnierg roup,[9g] albeit with moderate yields,
narrow substrate scope, and limited functional group compati-
bility (Scheme 1( A), bottom).

Our goal was to develop an orthogonal synthetic platform
to these efforts. In contrast to neutral allenes,a llenamides are
known to be activated by ar ange of electrophiles, such as
Lewis acids,B rønsted acids, and halonium reagents,t of orm
a,b-unsaturated iminium intermediates, which can then be in-
tercepted by various carbon and heteroatom (O or N) nucleo-
philes, including acids, alcohols, and amines.[10] We therefore
envisioneda ctivating the allenamide and trapping the result-
ing intermediate by as ingle reagent. Specifically,t he carboxylic
acid can protonate the allenamide to generate the reactive
iminium intermediate (A,S cheme 1( B)), which can then be in-
terceptb yt he generatedc arboxylate ion.
Results and Discussion
To develop the above proposed transformation,t he reactiono f
allene sulfonamide 1a with 1.3 equiv of benzoic acid (2a )i n
CH2Cl2 was first investigated (Table 1). To our delight, single
regio- ands tereoisomeric hydrocarboxylation product 3a was
obtainedi n7 4% yield with 23 %r ecovery of 1a when the reac-
tion mixture was stirred at room temperature for 24 h
(entry 1). The reaction yield improved slightly to 81 %w ith
complete conversion of 1a at 55 8Cw ithin 12 h( entry 2). The
use of other chlorinated solvents improved the yield to as high
as 97 %( entries 3a nd 4). Among the other tested solvents (en-
tries 5–9), acetonitrile gave similarr esults, although with a
longer incubation time (24 h). Changing to an alcohol solvent
system did not improve the yield of hydrocarboxylation pro-
duct 3a (entries 10–12). Reaction with EtOAc was sluggish,
with a6 7% yield after two days (entry 13). We recognize that
acetonitrile is environmentally more compatible than chlorinat-
ed solvents. In this work, we relied on DCE (entry 3) because of
the faster reaction time.
With these optimized conditions in hand, the generality of
the synthesis of trans g-acyloxyenamides 3 wase xamined
using various 18,2 8,a nd 38 carboxylic acids 2 (Table 2). In gen-
eral, all carboxylic acids reacted smoothly,r egardless of the
steric and electronic effects present.S pecifically,a ryl carboxylic
acids with one or two electron-donatingg roups (Me, OMe), an
electron-withdrawing group (Br,C l, I, Ph, and NO2), or both an
electron-donating and electron-withdrawing group (Me and
Br) positioned anywhereo nt he aryl ring were suitables ub-
strates for this reaction (3b –h). Various phenylacetic acid deriv-
atives were also effective and delivered the corresponding hy-
drocarboxylation products, 3i –k,i ns imilar yields (90–91 %).
The reactionw as also compatible with aliphatic carboxylic
acids irrespectiveo ft he nature or degree of a-substitution
(3l –o). Similarly,u nsaturated carboxylica cids featuring ap roxi-
mal unsaturation (3p ), ad istal unsaturation (3r ), and an unsa-
turationi na bridged carbocycle (3q )a nd af atty acid (linoleic
acid, 3s )w ere all suitable coupling partners;n os ide reactions
or geometrici somerization occurred. Bromo groups, a-hydrox-
yl groups at stereocenters,a nd phenolic groups were also
compatible (3t –v). It is worth mentioningt hat the hydroxyl
group of 2v did not lower the chemoselectivity[11] preference
for the acid, and the reaction proceeded rapidlyt og ive the de-
sired product within 30 min. These reaction conditions were
fully compatible with mono-N-protected a-aminoa cids;b enzo-
yl (on glycine), acetyl (on phenylalanine), and carbonate (on
leucine and proline) protecting groups were all well tolerated
under the standard conditions (3w –z). Most notably,t he inert-
ness of the halogen functionalities under these reaction condi-
tions allows for significant facile post-functionalization using
cross-coupling methodologies.

boxylic acids (Table2 (A), top right). Hydrocarboxylation was ef-

Due to the remarkable functional group tolerance, exclusive
selectivity,a nd promising yields, we were interested in late-
stage modification of complexm olecules rich in functional
groups and complexity (Table 2( A), bottom right). We therefore

worthy that enoxolone, ac hiral tertiaryc arboxylic acid, also re-

formed effectivelyi nto the enamide adducts with perfect
chemo-, regio-, and stereoselectivity (3a g–an); the various
functionalities such as ethers, thioethers, esters, lactones,a ce-
tals, amides,o lefins, and alcohols/phenols werei nert under the
reactionc onditions, further demonstratingt he synthetic utility
of this transformation in complex scenarios. We next focused
on expanding the generality of this transformation with other
diversea llenamide derivatives (Table 2( B)). As with the allene
of N-benzyl toluenesulfonamide (1a ), allenamides bearing neu-
tral or electron-rich aryls (1b and 1c ), allyl (1d ), nitrosulfonyl
(1e ), acyclico rc yclic carbamates (1f and 1g ), or cyclic amide
(1h )g roups were also suitable substrates and efficientlyc ou-
pled with benzoic acid with similarr eactivity and selectivity
(3a o–au). Unfortunately,a llenyl phosphine oxide did not react
to give 3a v,w hile the allenyl ether 1a w gave ac omplex mix-
ture.
We used density functional theoryc omputations in order to
elucidatet he mechanism in this transformation.T he structures,
energies, and thermal corrections were computed at the PBE/
6-31G* with SMD solvationc orrections for DCE.[12] We comput-
ed the complete reaction coordinate diagram for 3a u involv-
ing the oxazolidinone allenamide and benzoic acid. Four po-
tentialt ransition states rangingf rom concerted to stepwise
mechanisms are shown in Figure 1. The most direct path to
the experimentally observed g-acyloxyenamides would be the
concerted addition of the carboxylic acid O@Hb ond across the
terminal alkene of the allenamide (Concerted-1,2). Alternative-
ly,t he addition could occur in a1 ,4 fashion where the oxygen
involved in the nucleophilica ttack is distal to the OH involved
in the protonation event( Concerted-1,4). As tepwise process
is also possible (Carboxylation First vs. Protonation first). DFT
computations revealed that the concerted process is not possi-
ble. The Concerted-1,2 transition state was not as tationary
point on the potential energy surface, and the Concerted-1,4
transition state was geometrically impossible because the car-
boxylic acid group could not simultaneously reach the proto-
nation and carboxylation sites. In the stepwise mechanisms,
the Carboxylation First process did not lead to as table inter-
mediate—itm onotonically fragmentedb ack to the starting
allenamide and carboxylic acid.
The only viable mechanismw as the ProtonationF irst path-
way,w here the carboxylic acidf irst activates the allenamide
through protonation (Figure 2). The protonation of the allena-
mide had ab arrier of 14.5 kcal mol@1 (Cis-Prot-TS), which led
to the formation of the Iminium-Carboxylate complex (DG =
3.6 kcal mol@1). This intermediate readily collapses to the prod-
uct via 1,4-addition of the carboxylate to the vinylogousi mini-
um terminus( DG = @20.2 kcal mol@1).
We juxtaposed our methodology to the work by Monnier
(Table 3).[9g] Our methodology uniformly resulted in moderate
to excellent yields (70–97 %). In comparison, the Cu-catalyzed
hydrocarboxylation struggled with sterically hindered tertiary
carboxylica cids, which were either completely unreactive (3o
and 3a n)o rl ed to moderate yields (3h )( Table 3, entries 1, 2,
and 7). In addition, a,b-unsaturated and indole-tethered acids
(3p and 3a f,e ntries 3a nd 4) were found to be partially incom-
patible with Cu-catalysis, as the former substrate polymerizes
and the latter substrate deactivates the catalystt hrough N-che-
lation. Other sensitive functional groups incompatiblew ith
transition metal catalysts such as the cyclic disulfideo fl ipoic
acid,[13] base-sensitive acyclica nd cyclic esters, and hydroxy
groups were not viable under the copper-catalyzed conditions;
almostn op roduct was formed in the case of 3a g and 3a k
(entries 5a nd 6). Lastly,h ighly functionalized tertiary carboxylic
acid 3a n didn ot afford the corresponding product under Cu
catalysis (entry 7). In entries 8–11, we directly used the Monnier
copperr eactions ubstrates (3a o–au)i no rder to directly com-
pare the efficiencies of the reactions. In our hands, the metal-
free protocol consistently gave highery ields.

Conclusions
We disclose am etal-free, mild, operationally simple hydrocar-
boxylation method with exclusive chemo-,r egio-, and stereo-
control.D FT results show that the linear-selectiveh ydrocarbox-
ylationr eactionp roceeds in as tepwise manner through the in-
termediacy of ac onjugated iminium species, which gives rise
to as mall interception barrier for the carboxylate ion to react.
This atom-economical methodc an access ab road substrate
scope, affording aw idev ariety of trans-g-acyloxy-enamides in
excellent yields.T his coupling installs trans-propenamide unit
in to carboxylic acid feedstocks proceeds with excellent func-
tional group compatibility.F inally,t he combined advantages of
this methodology also allow ready access to late-stage func-
tionalization of complex natural products bearing carboxylic
acids, thereby enabling ample opportunity for facile down-
stream exploration and optimization of SAR.

Highly Chemoselective Esterification from O-Aminoallylation of
Carboxylic Acids:M etal- and Reagent-Free Hydrocarboxylation of
Allenamides
TapasR .P radhan+,[a] Hae Eun Lee+,[a] Gisela A. Gonzalez-Montiel,[b] Paul Ha-Yeon Cheong,*[b]
and Jin Kyoon Park*[a]
Abstract: Metal-free hydrocarboxylation of allenamides with
various functionalized carboxylic acids were achieved with
complete regio- and stereocontrol (> 49:1). This environ-
mentally compatible transformation affords g-acyloxyen-
amides with exclusive E-selectivity.E lectron rich, electron
poor,a liphatic, aryl, and heterocyclic carboxylic acids all
gave excellent yields (avg. 89 %, 47 examples). We demon-
strate the synthetic potentialo ft his transformation in the
late-stage modification of complex natural carboxylic acids
and simple modification of the products to three-carbon
synthons with ample opportunity for further diversification.
DFT studies revealed that the reaction occurs in as tepwise
mannert hrough the intermediacy of ac onjugated iminum
species, which is rapidly captured by the carboxylate ion, re-
sulting in the observed linear selectivity.
Introduction
The importance of ester groups has been highlighted by many
applicationsi nd rug discovery,[1] polymerization,[2] and electron-
ic material development.[3] Enamide groups have received par-
ticular attention as versatile ambiphilic building blocks[4] for
biologically relevant molecules, including therapeutically im-
portant natural products and drug molecules.[5] Herein, we dis-
close am ethodf or the direct O-aminoallylation of carboxylic
acid groups using allenamides to afford highly functionalizable
enamide derivatives.[6] This atom-economical method exhibits
ab road substrate scope, exclusive chemo-, regio-, and E-selec-
tivities. Our processt ransforms several inexpensive, stable, and
abundant carboxylic acids into synthetically valuable g-acyloxy-
enamides.T he mild reactionc onditions, exclusivec hemoselec-
tivity,a nd wide functional group tolerance also provide ready
access to late-stage functionalization of complex natural prod-
ucts bearing carboxylic acids. This chemoselective functionali-
zation is ap owerful way to construct libraries of novel chemi-
cal entities from simple and complex carboxylic acid sub-
strates,[7] enabling rapid exploration for structure–activity rela-
tionship (SAR).
The uniquec hemical features of allenes have inspired nu-
merous atom- and step-economic strategies for constructing
organic compounds including valuable synthons and polyfunc-
tional structures.[8] Despite the great success of transition-
metal catalysis, sustainable metal-free processes are increasing-
ly in demand because of clear disadvantages of metals, such
as:t oxicityo fm etals, cost and poor availability of ligands, and
hazardousness of additives. Meanwhile, Brønsted acid electro-
philic activation of allenesa sa greener alternative to transition
metal functionalization are relativelyr are.[9] In particular, hydro-
carboxylation, which enables the synthesis of linear or
brancheda llyl ester derivatives, under metal-free conditions re-
mains unknown (Scheme 1( A)). We report herein ag reener al-
ternative to the currents tate-of-the-art process, am etal-free
hydrocarboxylation (Scheme 1( B)), which could be used for ef-
ficientl ate-stage functionalization.
Transition-metal catalysts typically activate neutral
(Scheme 1( A), top). For example, iridium and rhodium[9b,c] cata-
lyst processes that produce branched products have been re-
portedi ndependently by Krische[9a] and Breit.[9b,c] On the other
hand, regiocontrolled synthesis of linear products with trans
selectivity from allenesh as been realizedb yG uo[9d] and Yama-
moto,[9e,f] using silver and palladium catalysts, respectively.
Most interestingly,l iteratures on transformationsi nvolving the
allenamides are scarce. The one exception is the recent report
of ac opper-catalyzed hydrocarboxylation of allenamides dis-
covered by the Monnierg roup,[9g] albeit with moderate yields,
narrow substrate scope, and limited functional group compati-
bility (Scheme 1( A), bottom).

Our goal was to develop an orthogonal synthetic platform
to these efforts. In contrast to neutral allenes,a llenamides are
known to be activated by ar ange of electrophiles, such as
Lewis acids,B rønsted acids, and halonium reagents,t of orm
a,b-unsaturated iminium intermediates, which can then be in-
tercepted by various carbon and heteroatom (O or N) nucleo-
philes, including acids, alcohols, and amines.[10] We therefore
envisioneda ctivating the allenamide and trapping the result-
ing intermediate by as ingle reagent. Specifically,t he carboxylic
acid can protonate the allenamide to generate the reactive
iminium intermediate (A,S cheme 1( B)), which can then be in-
terceptb yt he generatedc arboxylate ion.
Results and Discussion
To develop the above proposed transformation,t he reactiono f
allene sulfonamide 1a with 1.3 equiv of benzoic acid (2a )i n
CH2Cl2 was first investigated (Table 1). To our delight, single
regio- ands tereoisomeric hydrocarboxylation product 3a was
obtainedi n7 4% yield with 23 %r ecovery of 1a when the reac-
tion mixture was stirred at room temperature for 24 h
(entry 1). The reaction yield improved slightly to 81 %w ith
complete conversion of 1a at 55 8Cw ithin 12 h( entry 2). The
use of other chlorinated solvents improved the yield to as high
as 97 %( entries 3a nd 4). Among the other tested solvents (en-
tries 5–9), acetonitrile gave similarr esults, although with a
longer incubation time (24 h). Changing to an alcohol solvent
system did not improve the yield of hydrocarboxylation pro-
duct 3a (entries 10–12). Reaction with EtOAc was sluggish,
with a6 7% yield after two days (entry 13). We recognize that
acetonitrile is environmentally more compatible than chlorinat-
ed solvents. In this work, we relied on DCE (entry 3) because of
the faster reaction time.
With these optimized conditions in hand, the generality of
the synthesis of trans g-acyloxyenamides 3 wase xamined
using various 18,2 8,a nd 38 carboxylic acids 2 (Table 2). In gen-
eral, all carboxylic acids reacted smoothly,r egardless of the
steric and electronic effects present.S pecifically,a ryl carboxylic
acids with one or two electron-donatingg roups (Me, OMe), an
electron-withdrawing group (Br,C l, I, Ph, and NO2), or both an
electron-donating and electron-withdrawing group (Me and
Br) positioned anywhereo nt he aryl ring were suitables ub-
strates for this reaction (3b –h). Various phenylacetic acid deriv-
atives were also effective and delivered the corresponding hy-
drocarboxylation products, 3i –k,i ns imilar yields (90–91 %).
The reactionw as also compatible with aliphatic carboxylic
acids irrespectiveo ft he nature or degree of a-substitution
(3l –o). Similarly,u nsaturated carboxylica cids featuring ap roxi-
mal unsaturation (3p ), ad istal unsaturation (3r ), and an unsa-
turationi na bridged carbocycle (3q )a nd af atty acid (linoleic
acid, 3s )w ere all suitable coupling partners;n os ide reactions
or geometrici somerization occurred. Bromo groups, a-hydrox-
yl groups at stereocenters,a nd phenolic groups were also
compatible (3t –v). It is worth mentioningt hat the hydroxyl
group of 2v did not lower the chemoselectivity[11] preference
for the acid, and the reaction proceeded rapidlyt og ive the de-
sired product within 30 min. These reaction conditions were
fully compatible with mono-N-protected a-aminoa cids;b enzo-
yl (on glycine), acetyl (on phenylalanine), and carbonate (on
leucine and proline) protecting groups were all well tolerated
under the standard conditions (3w –z). Most notably,t he inert-
ness of the halogen functionalities under these reaction condi-
tions allows for significant facile post-functionalization using
cross-coupling methodologies.

boxylic acids (Table2 (A), top right). Hydrocarboxylation was ef-
ficient regardless of the electronic nature( O, S, or N), position,
